problem: The set-builder example {x : x is even and x < 10} = {2,4,6,8} never states the domain. As written, 0, -2, -4 ... also satisfy the rule, so the listed roster is only correct if x ranges over positive integers. A student copying this into an exam answer loses marks.
fix: State the domain: {x ∈ ℤ⁺ : x is even and x < 10} = {2,4,6,8}, where ℤ⁺ is the set of positive integers.

problem: "3 ∈ S, and if x ∈ S then x + 3 ∈ S, so S contains all positive multiples of 3" is true but incomplete: the rule alone allows larger sets such as {3,6,9,...} ∪ {100}. Only the smallest set closed under the rule is the multiples of 3.
fix: Say: 3 ∈ S, and if x ∈ S then x + 3 ∈ S. The smallest set satisfying this rule is S = {3,6,9,12,...}; any set satisfying the rule must contain all positive multiples of 3.

problem: "Some syllabi call it Boolean sum" is ambiguous: in Boolean algebra the Boolean sum is OR, i.e. union, and students who meet switching algebra later will read the term the other way. Most books call A △ B the ring sum or mod-2 sum.
fix: Write: some books call it the ring sum (or mod-2 sum), because it behaves like addition modulo 2.

problem: "A pair is not a set: (2,4) ≠ (4,2)" can be misread as denying that ordered pairs have any set definition, and the real point (order matters) is buried.
fix: Write: an ordered pair (2,4) is not the same as the two-element set {2,4}; order matters in a pair, so (2,4) ≠ (4,2), while {2,4} = {4,2}.
